1943

Alma Tharp Joins Memminger High School Victory Corps — World War II Community Service

March 9, 1943
Charleston, SC
Alma B

Newspaper article announcing the formation of a Victory Corps unit at Memminger High School in Charleston, South Carolina, as part of the school's contribution to the World War II home-front effort. The program was designed to train high-school students for future war service while encouraging active participation in community wartime activities. Students were required to meet academic, physical-training and community-service standards. Activities included Red Cross work, Civilian Defense assistance, USO support, rationing-board work, selling war bonds and stamps, victory gardens, and other wartime service projects. Among the students listed as enrolling in the Victory Corps is Alma Thorp [Tharp], who attended Memminger High School before becoming known for her aviation activities and membership in The Ninety-Nines.

Alma Tharp Serves in Memminger Victory Corps Nurses Aides Squad

Circa May 1943
Charleston, SC
Alma B

Newspaper article reporting the organization and officers of the Memminger Victory Corps at Memminger High School in Charleston, South Carolina. The corps was divided into specialized squads supporting community and wartime service activities, including the USO, Victory Gardens, Red Cross, clerical and library work, and nurses' aide service. Alma Tharp is specifically listed as a member of the First Platoon Nurses Aides Squad, along with Marie Petit, Sylvia Ginsberg, Virginia Burdashaw, Eloise Adams, Edna Hill, and Helen Hill. The article notes that Victory Corps members drilled each Tuesday under the direction of M. Simon Fogarty and Mr. Utsey of the Home Guard. Girls who completed 25 hours of community service and physical fitness work were presented with official Victory Corps insignia.

Alma Tharp Memorabilia — Clemson Dances and Middleton Place Gardens

Circa 1947
Charleston, SC
Alma B

Collection of personal keepsakes preserved among Alma Edythe Tharp's papers, including two invitations from The Central Dance Association at Clemson, South Carolina, and an admission pass to Middleton Place Gardens near Charleston. The Clemson invitations are for an Autumn Ball, held November 21–22 at the College Fieldhouse with music by Billy Knauff, and a Rat Hop, held October 3–4 at the College Fieldhouse with music by The Jungaleers. The invitations specify formal or semi-formal Friday-night dances followed by informal Saturday-night events. The Middleton Place Gardens pass is handwritten for “Miss Alma Tharp and one guest” and appears to have been issued on a complimentary basis.

Alma Tharp at Folly Beach — Miss American Legion Beauty Contest and Mr. Folly Beach

August 17, 1947
Alma B

Two newspaper clippings documenting Alma Tharp's involvement in Folly Beach community events. Folly Beach Float Wins at Tenth Annual Azalea Festival — Alma Tharp Represented as Queen

April 13, 1948
Charleston, SC
Alma B

Newspaper coverage of the Tenth Annual Azalea Festival parade in Charleston, South Carolina, attended by an estimated 80,000 spectators. More than 100 beauty representatives, including 28 official queens, participated along with 25 floats, 11 bands, and other parade units. The Folly Beach float, on which Alma Tharp served as queen, was judged the winning entry in the towns category. The article describes the float as featuring a large silver-and-green fan and identifies Alma's attendants as June Lockwood, Rose Marie Frost, Mary Lou Barnett, and Stella Barnett. Delores Jowers and Ann Angel rode at the front of the float. The accompanying article, “Queens Have Really Busy Day Ahead,” describes the schedule of activities arranged for the festival's 28 official queens, including a press conference, visits to Charleston's gardens, a hospital appearance, luncheon, and participation in festival events.

Alma Tharp Named Queen of Folly Beach Azalea Festival Float

April 14, 1948
Charleston, SC
Alma B

Collection of newspaper clippings and photographs documenting Alma Tharp's selection as Queen of the Folly Beach Azalea Festival float. Alma, identified as the 21-year-old daughter of G. E. Tharp of Folly Beach, won a beauty contest and dance held at the Folly Beach Community Center and was chosen to ride in the place of honor on the community's Azalea Festival parade float. Her court consisted of June Lockwood, runner-up; Rose Marie Frost; Mary Lou Barnett; and Stella Barnett. One article identifies Burnette Spencer as Alma's secretary during the event and reports that Alma was crowned by contest judge C. Wayne Cox. The clippings also provide important biographical details about Alma. She was a graduate of Memminger High School, was employed by the Hay Oil Company, owned her own airplane, and held a private pilot's license. The accompanying photographs show Alma wearing her crown and formal gown following her selection as Miss Folly Beach and Queen of the Folly Beach Azalea Festival float.

1949

Alma Tharp and The Ninety-Nines — Carolina Women Pilots and Air Race, 1949

May 21, 1949
Charleston, SC
Alma B

Collection of May 1949 newspaper clippings documenting Alma Tharp's aviation activities and involvement with the Carolinas Chapter of The Ninety-Nines, the international organization of licensed women pilots. A May 21, 1949 News and Courier article records Alma receiving her private pilot license at Carolina Skyways Airport. That same weekend, Alma flew her trim Ercoupe from Charleston to Spartanburg for the Carolinas Chapter's annual meeting. Other clippings identify her alongside fellow women pilots including Jewell Bailey. The chapter meetings included planning for the upcoming All-Woman Transcontinental Air Race, scheduled to begin in San Diego on June 11 and finish in Greenville, South Carolina. Charleston was selected as the race's eastern continental marker, requiring competitors to fly through Charleston before proceeding to Greenville. Dates represented: May 21 and May 25, 1949.

Ninety-Nines Women Pilots, 1950

May 31, 1950
Charleston, SC
Alma B

Newspaper clippings and a Carolinas Chapter newsletter document Alma Tharp of Folly Beach, South Carolina, as an active member of The Ninety-Nines, the international organization of licensed women pilots. In 1950, Alma was described as the youngest member of the Southeastern section of the two Carolinas. She and fellow Charleston pilot Jewell Bailey represented the organization at aviation events and conventions, including the Southeastern convention in Brunswick, Georgia, and had previously served as hostesses at the national Ninety-Nines convention in Greenville. The Carolinas Chapter newsletter also identifies Alma as a “99er from Charleston” and reports that she won a prize at an S.C. Breakfast Club meeting at Newberry for flying the greatest distance to attend. Together, the items document Alma's active participation in South Carolina aviation and the organized community of women pilots during 1950. Dates visible on the archive page: May 31, 1950 and September 5, 1950.

1952

Aviatrix Wed — Alma Edythe Tharp Marries James Stewart “Buster” Bell Jr.

Circa May 1952
Alma B

Newspaper announcement of the marriage of Alma Edythe Tharp of Folly Beach, South Carolina, to James Stewart Bell Jr. of Lancaster, South Carolina, on April 28 at Heath Springs. Alma, a graduate of Memminger High School, had been flying for six years, owned her own airplane, and held a private pilot’s license. She was a member of the Charleston Civil Air Patrol and was described as the youngest member in the Carolinas of The Ninety-Nines, an international organization of women pilots. James Stewart Bell Jr., son of Mrs. James S. Bell and the late Mr. Bell of Lancaster, had served four years in the U.S. Marines and was employed at Grace Bleachery in Lancaster, where the couple planned to live.

Carolina Women Pilots Hold Gathering at Folly Beach — Alma Tharp Hosts Ninety-Nines

Circa July 1952
Alma B

Newspaper article and group photograph documenting a quarterly meeting of the Carolinas Chapter of the Southeastern Section of The Ninety-Nines, the international organization of licensed women pilots. Lancaster Girl Pilot Proves Woman’s Place Is in Airplane — Alma Bell and Her Ercoupe

Circa August 1956
Lancaster County, SC
Alma B

The Lancaster News profile of Alma Edythe Tharp Bell (Mrs. Buster Bell) of Lancaster, South Carolina, describing her extensive involvement in aviation. The article reports that Alma had been flying since age 14, had accumulated approximately 500 flying hours, and at age 24 was teaching her husband, James Stewart “Buster” Bell Jr., to fly in preparation for his pilot’s license. Alma owned an Ercoupe two-seat airplane and was the only Lancaster woman known to belong to The Ninety-Nines, the international organization of licensed women pilots. She had been a member for five years and also belonged to the Civil Air Patrol and the South Carolina Breakfast Club. The article recalls that Alma's father initially objected to her interest in flying but later took lessons himself, obtained his pilot's license, and bought an airplane. At the time of the article, Alma and Buster were living at 407 East Gay Street in Lancaster. Alma worked in the order department of Springs Cotton Mills and continued flying with Buster on weekends.

William “Dickey” Bell — First Grade Report Card, Erwin School, 1962–1963

Circa June 1963
Erwin Elementary School, Lancaster County, SC
Dickey B

First-grade report card for William “Dickey” Bell from Erwin School, Lancaster City Schools, Lancaster, South Carolina, for the 1962–1963 school year. His teacher was Nancy L. Graham, and the principal was Mrs. T. K. Cunningham. At the end of the year, Dickey was assigned to second grade. Dickey earned A grades in Arithmetic, Reading, Writing, Science, and Health, with a final citizenship grade of B. The report records 180 days present, no absences, and no tardies for the school year. His habits and attitudes were marked satisfactory in nearly every category, including completing his work, following directions, respecting others, working independently, and caring for books and property. The one recurring area marked “Needs Improvement” was controlling talking and whispering. The report card contains several parent signatures of James S. Bell, providing an additional family record connected with Dickey's elementary-school years.

Farm League Tigers Defeat Dickey Bell’s Yankees, 18–12

June 20, 1963
Dickey B

Newspaper article reporting a Farm League baseball game at Hunter Field in which the Tigers defeated the Yankees, 18–12. The Tigers, managed by Don Scott and Dick Richards, earned their second consecutive victory after losing their first eleven games. Joe Simpson was the winning pitcher, while Sam Thomas, Randy Watts, and Gary Powell led the Tigers at the plate. Ray Bowers and Larry Blackwell were the leading Yankee hitters. The Yankees were coached by Bob Ackerman. Following the loss, the coaches and team were invited to Dickey Bell’s home, where they were treated to hot dogs to “soothe aching souls and wounded pride.”

1960s_0031.jpg
Download high resolution

Farm League Yankees Close Out Season — Dickey Bell Hosts Team Party

Circa July 1963
Dickey B

Newspaper article describing the final weeks of the Farm League Yankees' baseball season. The Yankees defeated the Red Sox 2–1 on Tuesday and defeated the Tigers twice, 4–0 on Wednesday and 6–2 on Thursday. On Wednesday night, Dickey Bell hosted a hot dog party at his home for the Yankees. Following Thursday's game, the team celebrated Ronnie Rogers' surprise birthday with Pepsi, cake, and ice cream. The article also records several team outings organized by Coach Bob Ackerman. On June 26, he took the players to Charlotte, North Carolina, to watch live championship wrestling at WBTV. The Yankees then planned a trip to Atlanta on July 6 and 7 to see the Atlanta Braves play.

William “Dickey” Bell — Third Grade Report Card, Erwin School, 1964–1965

Circa June 1965
Erwin Elementary School, Lancaster County, SC
Dickey B

Third-grade report card for William “Dickey” Bell from Erwin School, Lancaster City Schools, Lancaster, South Carolina, for the 1964–1965 school year. His teacher was Gladys R. Sims. At the completion of the school year, Dickey was assigned to fourth grade. Dickey had an exceptionally strong academic year, earning A's throughout the year in Arithmetic, Reading, Language, Writing, Spelling, Social Studies, Science, and Health. His year-end marks in these academic subjects were all A's. Citizenship was also consistently graded A. The report records 180 days present with no absences, giving Dickey perfect attendance for the school year. His habits and attitudes were marked satisfactory throughout, including courtesy, attentiveness, working independently, respecting authority, completing assignments, and working well with others. The report card contains repeated parent signatures of James S. Bell, including a more formal signature on the final report.

William “Dickey” Bell — Fourth Grade Report Card, Erwin School, 1965–1966

Circa June 1966
Erwin Elementary School, Lancaster County, SC
Dickey B

Fourth-grade report card for William “Dickey” Bell from Erwin School, Lancaster City Schools, Lancaster, South Carolina, for the 1965–1966 school year. His teacher was Julia R. Beckham. At the end of the school year, Dickey was promoted to fifth grade. Dickey continued to perform strongly academically, receiving predominantly A and B grades in Arithmetic, Reading, Language, Writing, Spelling, Social Studies/Geography, Science, and Health. His attendance was excellent, with the report showing 180 days present for the school year. The habits-and-attitudes section contains the handwritten teacher comment “Talks too much”. Early reporting periods also show areas needing improvement in interrupting, neatness, and attentiveness, with improvement evident later in the year. The report card contains several signatures of his father, James Stewart Bell Jr. The final report includes the humorous handwritten parental comment “That’s a laugh!” followed by his BROTHER's full signature.

Early reporting periods also show areas needing improvement in interrupting, neatness, and attentiveness, with improvement evident later in the year. The report card contains several signatures of his father, James Stewart Bell Jr. The final report includes the humorous handwritten parental comment “That’s a laugh!” followed by his BROTHER's full signature.

Marine Major John J. Tharp Returns Home After Being Wounded in Vietnam — March 8, 1968

March 8, 1968
Johnny Tharp

Globe newspaper article dated Friday, March 8, 1968, documenting the return of Marine Major John J. Tharp after he was wounded while serving as a helicopter pilot in Vietnam. Major Tharp had deployed to Vietnam in March 1967 and served with Marine Medium Helicopter Squadron HMM-165 aboard the USS Valley Forge. During a mission supporting Marines at the Huế Citadel, Tharp was piloting a CH-46 helicopter when enemy fire struck the aircraft and a round ricocheted into his leg. Despite being wounded, he turned the controls over to his copilot and was flown to Phu Bai, then evacuated through Cam Ranh Bay and Japan for further treatment. Major Tharp returned to the United States on February 28, 1968, approximately three weeks after being wounded. The accompanying photograph shows his reunion with his wife, Mrs. John J. Tharp, and their children, John Jr., age 7, and Lori, at the Marine Corps Air Facility, New River, North Carolina. The article recounts that before leaving for Vietnam, Tharp had reassured his family that he would return. His son John Jr. reportedly greeted him by saying, “No, Daddy, we just knew you would come home.”

Dickey Bell South Carolina Highway Patrol Speeding Warning – 1982

Circa 1982
Dickey B

South Carolina State Highway Patrol warning issued to William Richard “Dickey” Bell on April 10, 1982, in Lancaster County. Dickey was driving a 1979 Dodge on Highway 9 when he received a warning for speeding or driving too fast for conditions. The warning was issued by Patrolman M. E. Johnson and is another surviving piece documenting Dickey’s driving history.

Buster ObituraryJames S. “Buster” Bell Jr. Obituary – 1990

April 2, 1990
Buster B

Obituary for James S. “Buster” Bell Jr., 69, of Lancaster, South Carolina, who died Monday, April 2, 1990. A retired Springs Power Plant employee and World War II Marine Corps veteran, Buster was survived by his wife, Alma Tharp Bell; sons James S. Bell III and William R. “Dickey” Bell; two sisters, two brothers, and two grandchildren. Services were held at Mahaffey Funeral Home Chapel, with burial at Lancaster Memorial Park.

Alma Tharp Bell – A Lifetime of Aviation and a Record-Setting Legacy

May 19, 1994
Lancaster County, SC
Alma B

Retrospective newspaper article by J. Douglas Donehue recounting the aviation career of Alma Edythe Tharp Bell. Alma made her first solo flight at age 16 and became one of the relatively few licensed women pilots active in South Carolina during the late 1940s and early 1950s. She frequently flew with fellow aviator and close friend Jewell Bailey in Alma's airplane, named “Rebel” after Charleston's South Atlantic League baseball team. The article describes Alma and Jewell's involvement with The Ninety-Nines, the organization founded by Amelia Earhart and other women pilots. In 1949, Jewell Bailey set a light-airplane altitude record at the Azalea Festival, flying a Piper Cub to 26,875 feet, 1,112 feet above the previous record. In 1947, Alma flew her father, Graham Tharp, to Atlanta to see a new Ercoupe. He liked the airplane so much that he purchased it for Alma. Alma later taught her father to fly and also taught her 14-year-old brother Johnny Tharp. In 1950, she served as an official hostess for the national Ninety-Nines convention in Greenville and was described as the organization's youngest member. As Alma's reputation grew, she and Jewell Bailey became well known in regional aviation circles, flying to air shows throughout the Carolinas and Southeast. Alma grew up at Folly Beach, later married James Stewart “Buster” Bell Jr. in 1952, and moved to Lancaster. The article states that Alma was 67 years old when she died on May 19.

Alma Tharp Bell Memorial Obituary – 1994

May 20, 1994
Alma B

Memorial obituary for Alma Tharp Bell, published in The Enterprise of High Point, North Carolina, on May 20, 1994. Alma died May 18, 1994, at age 67. Born in Charleston to Graham E. and Ethel Fike Tharp, she later lived in Lancaster, worked for Springs Industries, and was a member of Christ Episcopal Church. She was the widow of James Stewart Bell Jr. and was survived by her sons James S. Bell III and William R. “Dickey” Bell, along with her siblings and two grandchildren. Alma was buried at Lancaster Memorial Park.

Alma B

Alma Tharp Bell Obituary – May 1994

May 20, 1994
Lancaster County, SC
Alma B

Newspaper obituary for Alma Tharp Bell, 67, of Lancaster, South Carolina, who died May 18, 1994. The notice identifies her as a Charleston County native, former Springs Industries employee, member of Christ Episcopal Church, and widow of James Stewart Bell Jr. It lists her sons James Bell III and William “Dickey” Bell, her brother Johnny Tharp, sisters Marion Brown and Rachel Bell, and two grandchildren. Funeral services were held at Mahaffey Funeral Home, with burial at Lancaster Memorial Park.

Technical Solutions – Bell Family Business – 1998

July 26, 1998
Dickey B, Rickey B, Stephanie B

July 26, 1998 Lancaster News feature on Technical Solutions, a Lancaster business equipment and computer company founded October 14, 1996, by Ricky Bell, Stephanie Bell, and Dickey Bell. The company sold and serviced Sharp copiers and fax machines and provided custom-built computers, networking, upgrades, and computer repair. The article also lists Ricky Bell as a service technician and Debbie Phillips as a member of the sales staff.

TSI.jpg
Download high resolution

Rickey and Stephanie Bell at Technical Solutions – 1998

September 23, 1998
Rickey B, Stephanie B

September 23, 1998 newspaper business feature showing Ricky and Stephanie Bell, owners of Technical Solutions in Lancaster, South Carolina, searching for Sharp copier parts on a computer. Technical Solutions sold, leased, rented, and serviced Sharp copiers and fax machines while also providing custom-built computers, computer networking, and technical service.

Dickey Bell’s Work Cubicle at Springs Industries – Early 2000s

August 20, 2002
Dickey B

Photographs of William Richard “Dickey” Bell’s work cubicle at Springs Industries, where he worked in information systems and customer service. His workspace was filled with family photographs, academic and professional mementos, and awards collected over the years. Prominently displayed was his Springs Industries Twenty-Five Year Club certificate honoring his service since 1977. The photographs provide a personal look at Dickey’s workplace and the long career he built with Springs.

Jason Hoke Funeral Last Call

October 3, 2017
Jason Hoke

Lancaster dispatch couldn't make the last call at the funeral because he had left Lancaster for Chester. Rickey made the call using two handheld radios and Chester's local frequencies so it wouldn't reach the Chester County repeaters. Many on- and off-duty responders attended the funeral with pagers; the plan was for the Chester pagers to go off and broadcast the call. For reasons that can not be explained, EVERY pager at the funeral went off and broadcast the call, regardless of county, frequency, or service. It was really like God himself was sending Jason home!

BQ1 – Gilliam-McConnell Airfield

March 9, 2023

BQ1 is one of those airports that makes a great excuse to go flying. Located in Carthage, North Carolina, the real attraction is that you can land, park the airplane, and walk right over to the BBQ restaurant on the field. It’s a perfect fly-in destination: grab some barbecue, watch airplanes come and go, and then head back home. Sometimes the best reason for a flight is simply BBQ at the end of the runway. BQ1 – Fly in. Eat BBQ. Fly home.

The First Solo – Cutting the Shirt Tail

April 3, 2023
Confederate Ave, Lancaster County, SC
Rickey B

One of aviation’s oldest traditions happens after a student pilot completes their first solo flight. In the early days of flying, instructors often sat behind their students in tandem aircraft. With no radios or intercoms, the instructor would sometimes get the student’s attention by tugging on the back of their shirt. Once the student successfully flew alone, they no longer needed the instructor pulling on their shirttail. So after that first solo, the instructor cuts the tail off the student pilot’s shirt. The shirttail is usually dated and marked with the aircraft, airport, or other details from the flight and kept as a reminder of the accomplishment. For a pilot, that cut shirt represents something much bigger than an old piece of fabric—it marks the first time you took an airplane up, flew it, and brought it safely back down completely on your own. Your first solo is a flight you never forget.

Snorkeling for Scallops

July 3, 2023
Crystal River, FL
Rickey B

Scalloping is part treasure hunt, part fishing trip, and part underwater adventure. With a mask, snorkel, fins, and a mesh bag, you head into the clear, shallow water searching through the seagrass for bay scallops. Once you spot one, you dive down and pick it up by hand—but watch your fingers, because they can snap their shells shut! It’s a great way to spend a summer day on the water, and there’s nothing quite like bringing the day’s catch back to the boat and later enjoying fresh scallops that you collected yourself. Swim. Search. Dive. Dinner.

Cedar Key, Florida – Fly-In Adventure

February 7, 2024
FL

Flying into Cedar Key, Florida is an adventure all by itself. The small island airport sits right along the Gulf, giving you beautiful views of the water and islands as you come in to land. After tying down the airplane, you can head into town for fresh seafood, cold drinks, and that laid-back Old Florida atmosphere Cedar Key is known for. It’s not about getting somewhere fast—it’s about enjoying the flight, the scenery, and arriving somewhere you probably wouldn't experience the same way by car. Fly in. Eat seafood. Enjoy the island. Fly home.

KSSI – Fly-In BBQ

May 3, 2024
Mike Morgan, Sabrina Odem

KSSI – Fly-In BBQ Sometimes the best flying destinations are the simple ones: an airplane, a runway, and good BBQ. A flight into KSSI – St. Simons Island Airport combines the fun of flying with one of aviation’s favorite traditions—going somewhere just because there’s something good to eat when you get there. Land the airplane, tie it down, grab some BBQ, enjoy St. Simons Island for a while, and then climb back in for the flight home. Because pilots will fly a long way for good BBQ.

William Richard “Dickey” Bell Sr. Death Certificate – 2026

Circa July 2026
Dickey B

Official State of South Carolina death certification for William Richard “Dickey” Bell Sr., who died at his home in Lancaster on July 1, 2026, at age 69. The certificate records his birth on August 15, 1956, identifies his parents as James Stewart Bell Jr. and Alma Tharp, and lists his wife, Sonja Barnett Bell, as the informant. The document serves as the official vital record of Dickey’s death and was issued by the South Carolina Department of Public Health on July 20, 2026.

William Richard “Dickey” Bell Sr. Obituary – 2026

July 8, 2026
Dickey B

July 8, 2026 Lancaster News obituary for William Richard “Dickey” Bell Sr., 69, of Lancaster, South Carolina, who died July 1, 2026. Born August 15, 1956, Dickey was the son of James Stewart “Buster” Bell Jr. and Alma Tharp Bell and brother of James Stewart “Spooky” Bell III. He was a member of the Church of the Good Shepherd and was survived by his wife, Sonja Barnett Bell, his son Rickey Bell and wife Stephanie, two grandchildren, and three great-grandchildren.
